directions: Plant bare-root or container trees in late winter or early spring in deep, well-drained, fertile soil in full sun with a compatible pollinizer. Discovered as a chance seedling on Jacob Tyson's Pennsylvania farm in 1794, Tyson bears small to medium yellow pears with a distinctive honeyed sweetness and fine, melting texture that made it a favored dessert pear among American orchardists for generations, even though its modest size kept it from ever becoming a major commercial variety. The tree is notably vigorous, productive, and disease-resistant compared to many European pears of its era, qualities that helped it persist in old homestead orchards long after flashier varieties fell out of favor. Harvest while still firm in late summer and ripen indoors at room temperature until the flesh yields to gentle pressure.

Harvest while still firm in early fall and ripen indoors at room temperature until the flesh yields to gentle pressure.

Raised by Francis Dana of Massachusetts in 1854, this heirloom bears small, yellow, lightly russeted pears that are widely considered among the richest and most refined-flavored of all American-bred pears, with dense, buttery, aromatic flesh that rewards patient ripening despite the fruit's unassuming size. Its late-season timing extends the home orchard's pear harvest well into the cooler months. Harvest while still firm in fall and ripen indoors at room temperature until the flesh yields to gentle pressure; the fruit stores and keeps notably well for a dessert pear.

common_name: Netted Gem Melon (Ancestor of the Modern Cantaloupe)

planting.note: Direct sow after soil has warmed following last frost; Netted Gem, introduced around 1881, is the historic Michigan-area heirloom widely credited as the direct ancestor of the modern netted commercial cantaloupe.

directions: Direct sow after the soil has warmed following the last frost, in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun. Introduced around 1881, Netted Gem produces small, round, densely netted fruit with sweet, salmon-orange flesh, and its heavy netting pattern and reliable sweetness made it enormously influential in American melon breeding — most of the netted cantaloupe types sold in grocery stores today trace back to selections made from this variety. The compact vines are productive and well suited to home gardens. Harvest when the fruit slips easily from the vine with gentle pressure and the netting has fully developed, indicating peak ripeness and sweetness.

planting.note: Direct sow after soil has warmed following last frost; Cole's Early was bred by A.B. Cole of Iowa in 1908 specifically to ripen watermelon reliably in a short northern growing season.

directions: Direct sow after the soil has warmed following the last frost, in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun. Bred by A.B. Cole in Iowa in 1908, this heirloom was developed specifically to bring reliable, sweet watermelon to gardeners in short-season Northern climates where later-maturing Southern varieties often failed to ripen before fall frost. It bears medium-sized, oval, dark green striped melons with crisp, sweet red flesh on vigorous, productive vines. Harvest when the tendril nearest the fruit has dried and browned and the underside spot has turned from white to cream-yellow, reliable signs of ripeness in a short-season melon bred for gardens with a narrow window to work with.
